title: On AI, Is It All or Nothing
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Petrilli gathers reader responses to the New York City and Los Angeles school AI bans and, unusually for him, comes down on the side of the blunt instrument. He concedes the case for nuance made by ed-tech advocates, who point out that a student outsourcing an essay and a teacher using AI to diagnose reading difficulty are not the same act, but argues that nuance without enforcement collapses back into the status quo. His reading of the two districts is that their leaders have admitted they cannot police the distinction, so a pause functions as first do no harm. He lets the strongest versions of both sides speak, from a PTSA technology chair on twenty years of ed-tech failure to Robert Pondiscio on AI feedback that expands teacher capacity, then locates the real issue in the absence of results-based accountability that would make trusting schools rational. The second half of the issue turns on Alpha School, where he stacks up critical accounts from Ben Riley, Van Schoales and Will Austin and warns against letting public money flow to unverified claims. A closing thread picks up Alexander Thompson's argument that blaming phones for PISA decline lets bad curriculum policy off the hook.
points: Argues that the nuanced compromise on school AI is unenforceable in practice, so a categorical pause is the more honest policy even though it sacrifices good tools.
Reads the New York and Los Angeles bans as district leaders conceding they cannot distinguish harmful from useful AI inside their own buildings.
Locates the root problem in accountability: without real consequences for low performance, there is no reason to trust that schools will pick tools that raise achievement.
Compiles three separate critiques of Alpha School, including boot-camp practices involving heart-rate monitoring and unverified claims of 99th percentile results at up to 75,000 dollars in tuition.
Amplifies the counterargument that pinning PISA decline on screens excuses the curriculum decisions education policymakers actually control.
quotes: On this one, I find myself in a strange place. Whereas my typical position as the “David Brooks of education policy” is to find a comfortable spot between the extremes, this time I find myself thinking that “all or nothing” is the better approach and that the “nuanced compromise” is unworkable.

Maybe we should read NYC’s and LAUSD’s actions as acknowledgments that district leaders are powerless to enforce nuance in their schools, at least as it pertains to AI. Maybe after pressing pause for a year, they will be able to separate the wheat from the chaff.
And I can imagine that schools of choice that embrace a back-to-basics, paper-and-pencil approach are going to do quite well in the years ahead—classical academies among them.
Terms like “screen time,” “ed tech,” and “AI” cram dozens of use cases into a single word.
Phones hijack the attention of adults as much as kids. Districts spent too much, too fast on ed tech with too little evidence. It’s all sort of maddening.

If we still had serious results-based accountability with real consequences for low performance, perhaps we could trust that schools would make good decisions, opting for tools that boost student achievement and avoiding ones that are simply distraction devices. But we don’t, so we can’t.
But that doesn’t mean the rest of us shouldn’t be skeptical, or that we shouldn’t worry about fraud, or that we should allow public funding to flow to these schools
Even if it “was the phones,” in part, we shouldn’t ignore the decisions that those of us in education policy have control over—especially what we ask students to study in school!
